title: Assembly Language Basics
summary: Reading and writing simple assembly, and mapping familiar C constructs onto the instructions they compile to.

slides.sectionTitle: Assembly as a view of machine code
slides.markdown:
**Assembly language** is a human-readable, near-1:1 stand-in for raw machine instructions — each assembly line typically maps to exactly one instruction word. It's the lowest level a human normally reads; below it is just bits.

Unlike C, assembly has **no expressions, no types beyond raw bit widths, and no automatic anything** — every register move, every memory access, every comparison is spelled out explicitly. This is exactly why reading it reveals what a language construct "really costs" in instructions.

A line of assembly has a predictable anatomy:

```
loop:   add  $t0, $t0, 1    # increment counter
```

- **Label** (`loop:`) — a named address other instructions can jump/branch to; it doesn't exist in the compiled binary, only in the listing.
- **Mnemonic** (`add`) — the human-readable name for an opcode.
- **Operands** (`$t0, $t0, 1`) — destination, source(s), following that ISA's argument order.
- **Comment** (`# ...`) — for humans only; the assembler ignores it entirely.

Once you know this shape, any unfamiliar ISA's listing becomes readable within minutes.

A simple C loop next to its compiled form:

```c
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    sum += i;
}
```

```asm
     li   $t0, 0        # i = 0
     li   $t1, 0        # sum = 0
loop_start:
     bge  $t0, 10, loop_end   # if i >= 10, exit
     add  $t1, $t1, $t0       # sum += i
     addi $t0, $t0, 1         # i++
     j    loop_start
loop_end:
```

Notice there's no `for` in the output at all — a `for` loop is purely a **source-level convenience**; the compiler unrolls it into an ordinary conditional-branch-back-to-a-label pattern.

Calling `int add(int a, int b)` and using its return value:

```asm
     li   $a0, 3        # arg0 = 3
     li   $a1, 4        # arg1 = 4
     call add           # jump, save return address
     move $t0, $v0       # capture return value
```

The pattern is universal across ISAs even though register names differ: **arguments go into designated registers, the call saves where to resume, and the return value comes back in a designated register** ($v0 here). This is the calling convention showing up in real code.

Not every line in an assembly listing is a real instruction. **Assembler directives** (`.data`, `.text`, `.word`) tell the assembler how to lay out memory, not what the CPU should execute. **Pseudo-instructions** (`li $t0, 5` — "load immediate") are conveniences the assembler *expands* into one or more real instructions behind the scenes.

On many RISC ISAs, `li` with a large constant silently expands into the `lui`+`addi` pair from the encoding topic — the assembler is doing real work you don't see, which matters when you're counting actual executed instructions.

Same x86 instructions, two different notations you'll meet in the wild:

| | AT&T syntax | Intel syntax |
|---|---|---|
| Operand order | source, destination | destination, source |
| Register prefix | `%eax` | `eax` |
| Immediate prefix | `$5` | `5` |
| Example | `movl $5, %eax` | `mov eax, 5` |
| Common in | GNU tools, Linux `gdb`/`objdump` default | Intel manuals, MASM, NASM, Windows tooling |

Both encode the *exact same instruction* — the difference is purely textual notation, not semantics. Know which one your debugger/disassembler is showing you before reading operand order.

slides.subTitle: Misreading operand order
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Assembly operand order is universal — the first operand is always the destination."

**Why it's wrong:** it's exactly backwards between the two common x86 notations. AT&T's `movl %eax, %ebx` moves **`eax` into `ebx`** (source first); Intel's `mov ebx, eax` means the **same operation**, but with destination first.

**Correct model:** always confirm which syntax you're reading before interpreting operand order — mixing them up silently swaps source and destination in your mental trace, which produces confidently wrong debugging conclusions.
